'''''Elaeagnus pungens''''' is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] Elaeagnaceae, known by the [[common name]]s '''thorny olive''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=ELPU2|taxon=Elaeagnus pungens|access-date=18 January 2016}}</ref> '''spiny oleaster'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> and '''silverthorn'''; also by the family name "oleaster". It is native to Asia, including China and Japan. It is present in the southeastern United States as an [[introduced species]], a common [[landscaping]] and [[ornamental plant]], and sometimes an [[invasive species]].<ref name=feis>Gucker, Corey L. (2011). [http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/shrub/elapun/all.html ''Elaeagnus pungens''.] In: Fire Effects Information System, [Online]. U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Research Station, Fire Sciences Laboratory. Retrieved 1 March 2012.</ref>

==Description==
''Elaeagnus pungens'' is a dense, branching [[shrub]] which can reach over {{convert|7|m|ft}} tall by {{convert|4|m|ft}} wide. It sprouts prolifically from its stem, spreading out and twining into adjacent vegetation. Parts of the stem are covered in [[thorns, spines, and prickles|thorns]] which can be up to {{convert|8|cm|in}} long. The evergreen, alternately-arranged leaves are up to {{convert|10|cm|in}} long but under {{convert|5|cm|in}} wide. The undersides are silvery white with brown flecks. Tubular flowers are borne in clusters of up to three.<ref name=feis/> The flowers are yellowish or white and are sweet-scented.<ref name=fla>[http://plants.ifas.ufl.edu/node/653 ''Elaeagnus pungens''.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120106164149/http://plants.ifas.ufl.edu/node/653 |date=6 January 2012 }} Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants, University of Florida IFAS. Retrieved 1 March 2012.</ref> The fruit is a [[drupe]] up to {{convert|1.5|cm|in}} long which contains one seed.<ref name=feis/> It is reddish with silver scales.<ref name=fla/> Blooming occurs in the autumn and fruit develops during the spring. The plant grows quickly, with shoots growing over one meter per season. The growth has been described as "aggressive", with shoots extending many meters into neighboring treetops. The seeds are [[seed dispersal|dispersed]] by birds.<ref name=feis/>

==Habitat==
In China this plant occurs on hillsides and in thickets. In Japan it grows in scrub dominated by ''[[Quercus phillyraeoides]]'' and ''[[Pittosporum tobira]]''. This plant was introduced to the United States from Asia in 1830. It has been used extensively as a landscaping plant. Its densely packed, spreading form has proved useful along roadsides and highway medians. It was also used to [[revegetation|revegetate]] abandoned mining sites in [[Kentucky]] and other areas. It took hold easily and still persists in these places. It also spread into the wild, having escaped cultivation. In [[North Carolina]] it has been reported from [[Pinus palustris|longleaf pine]] forests, urban and maritime forests, and [[quercus|oak]]-[[carya|hickory]] woodlands. In [[Alabama]] it grows in urban areas and in protected, natural habitats as a weed. The South Carolina Southern Weed Science Society places it as an invasive species in their local area.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Bodner |first1=Ted |title=Invasive Plant Pest Species of South Carolina |url=https://www.se-eppc.org/southcarolina/scinvasives.pdf}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
[[File:Elaeagnus pungens - JBM.jpg|thumbnail|right|''E. pungens'' as [[bonsai]], [[Montreal Botanical Garden]]]]
Despite its invasive potential, ''E. pungens'' is widely cultivated as a garden plant in [[temperateness|temperate]] regions. It tolerates varied environmental conditions, including heat, cold, wind, coastal conditions, shade, and full sun. It is very drought-tolerant. It can grow in varied soil types, including those found at mine spoils.<ref name=feis/> Numerous [[cultivar]]s have been developed, especially for [[variegation|variegated]] foliage effects. Commercially available [[cultivar]]s include 'Maculata', which has gold coloration on the leaves,<ref name=bbc>[https://www.bbc.co.uk/gardening/plants/plant_finder/plant_pages/283.shtml ''E. pungens'' 'Maculata'.] BBC Plant Finder. Retrieved 1 March 2012.</ref> as well as 'Fruitlandii', 'Hosoba-Fukurin'<ref name=nc>[http://www.ces.ncsu.edu/depts/hort/consumer/factsheets/shrubs/elaeagnus_pungens.html ''E. pungens''.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120701220616/http://www.ces.ncsu.edu/depts/hort/consumer/factsheets/shrubs/elaeagnus_pungens.html |date=1 July 2012 }} NC State University. Retrieved 1 March 2012.</ref> and 'Goldrim'.<ref>{{cite web|title=''Elaeagnus pungens'' 'Goldrim'|url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=692|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|access-date=25 July 2013}}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

[[Elaeagnus × submacrophylla|''Elaeagnus'' × ''submacrophylla'']], formerly known as ''E.'' × ''ebbingei'', is a hybrid between ''[[Elaeagnus macrophylla|E. macrophylla]]'' and ''E. pungens''. The hybrid and its [[cultivar]]s are also grown in gardens as ornamental plants.<ref name=Edwa17>{{Cite journal |last1=Edwards |first1=Dawn |date=2017 |title=A new name for an ''Elaeagnus'' hybrid |journal=The Plantsman |series=New Series |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=222–223 }}</ref>

==Ecology==
Many birds feed on the fruits of the shrub.  Birds are most attracted to the plants that produce the most fruit.<ref name=feis/> Studies have found that [[Cedar Waxwing|cedar waxwings]] attracted to roadside plantings of the shrub are susceptible to automobile-related mortality. In [[Brazos County, Texas]] between 8 March and 5 April 1981, researchers counted 298 cedar waxwings that had been killed while trying to get fruits from thorny-olive shrubs growing along one highway.<ref name=feis/>
